Hi there! I'm putting together a summer backyard barbecue for about 20 friends and family members, and I could use some help planning a menu that works well for both kids and adults.

A few mainstays that keep everyone happy include chilled bratwurst or chicken sausages that can be grilled and sliced, plus a big platter of corn on the cob brushed with a little butter and salt. You’ll also want a sturdy veggie tray with cucumbers, bell peppers, and cherry tomatoes so the kids can snack without making a mess.
Thanks for those ideas! How much food should I plan on per person if I'm offering a couple of main meat options plus sides and dessert?

Plan on about half a pound of cooked meat per adult, a quarter pound for the kids, and add an extra pound or two in total for second helpings after the sun is up. Keep sides at roughly one cup of cooked grain or vegetable per person, and dessert can be as simple as a single square of cake or a scoop of ice cream.
Hi, I'm planning a bathroom renovation and need some help choosing tiles—can you walk me through the main material options I should be considering?

Natural stone like slate or marble gives you a dramatic look, but you’ll need to reseal it every couple of years so it stays stain-resistant. Porcelain is denser and more scratch-proof, while ceramic is softer and more affordable but can chip if you drop something heavy. If you want the stone appearance without the upkeep, porcelain through-body tiles work well.
That helps, thanks—what are the main differences I should know about between ceramic and porcelain for a bathroom setting?

Ceramic is fired at a lower temperature, so it’s more porous and you’ll need to seal the grout carefully to keep water out. Porcelain is denser and nearly waterproof, making it safer for shower floors. Both can look identical, but porcelain costs a bit more upfront.
Hi there! I'm planning a Sunday family dinner and I'd love a simple roast chicken recipe that works well with a few side dishes.

Start with a three to four pound chicken, pat it dry, rub it with one tablespoon each of salt and pepper, then add two tablespoons of softened butter under the skin so the meat stays moist while the skin crisps up. Stuff the cavity with a half lemon, three thin onion slices, and a handful of fresh parsley to keep the flavor interesting without making things complicated.
Could you also suggest a couple of vegetable sides that would go nicely with it?

Roasting some potatoes and carrots on a sheet pan alongside the chicken is the easiest way to get everything done in one go. Toss the cut vegetables with a little oil, salt, and pepper, then arrange them around the chicken so they catch the drippings while the oven runs. You'll pick up the maximum flavor with minimal cleanup.
Hi there! I just got a 3-month-old Labrador puppy named Cooper and I'm trying to figure out the best puppy food brand to start with — can you recommend a few good options?

Cooper sounds like a handful in the best possible way, and starting with the right food really does matter at this stage. Look for anything that lists a named meat as the first ingredient, because that’s the clearest sign of quality protein, and aim for options with at least 22 percent crude protein and 8 percent fat to fuel his growth.
Thanks for those suggestions! How many times a day should I be feeding him at this age, and roughly how much per meal?

At three months Cooper still needs those small, frequent meals, so four feedings spread through the day will keep his energy steady and his stomach happy. Measure each portion by the serving chart on the bag you choose, but as a rule of thumb, give him about one and a half cups of dry food across all four meals, then adjust up or down depending on whether he comes back for seconds or leaves food behind.

Hi there! I'm putting together a summer backyard barbecue for about 20 friends and family members, and I could use some help planning a menu that works well for both kids and adults.

A great way to keep everyone happy is to build a menu around a few crowd-pleasing proteins and plenty of fresh sides that stay cool. Start with a simple grilled chicken or turkey burger station—offer both lean and standard patties, plus a vegetarian black bean option—and add a couple of kid-friendly skewers like small sausages and bell pepper chunks.
Thanks for those ideas! How much food should I plan on per person if I'm offering a couple of main meat options plus sides and dessert?

Aim for about four to six ounces of cooked protein per adult and two to three ounces per child, plus roughly two cups of total side dishes per person, and allow one to two dessert items per guest. A good starting point for twenty people would be two pounds of ground meat, a pound and a half of vegetarian patties, three pounds of skewer ingredients, four pounds of potatoes for salad, a gallon of coleslaw, and a dozen paper plates of brownie bites.
Hi, I'm planning a bathroom renovation and need some help choosing tiles—can you walk me through the main material options I should be considering?

You have three practical choices for bathroom tiles. Ceramic is the budget-friendly starter; it’s easy to cut and paint but chips if you drop something heavy on it. Porcelain is denser, resists scratches and water, and can mimic stone or concrete without the upkeep. Natural stone such as slate or travertine adds character but needs sealing twice a year and costs more upfront.
That helps, thanks—what are the main differences I should know about between ceramic and porcelain for a bathroom setting?

Ceramic tiles are made from lower-fired clay, which makes them lighter and easier to cut with a basic snap cutter. Porcelain tiles are fired at higher temperatures and compressed harder, giving them a denser body that resists water absorption and scratches. In a wet room you’ll notice porcelain stays dry longer and lasts longer without grout lines turning gloomy.
Hi there! I'm planning a Sunday family dinner and I'd love a simple roast chicken recipe that works well with a few side dishes.

A simple roast chicken starts with a whole three-to-four-pound bird, patted dry and seasoned with salt, pepper, and a little olive oil. Tuck lemon halves and a few sprigs of thyme inside, then place it upright on the rack so the heat circulates evenly. Roast at 425°F for about an hour and fifteen minutes, letting the skin brown and crisp while the juices stay inside.
Could you also suggest a couple of vegetable sides that would go nicely with it?

Roasted root vegetables like carrots, parsnips, and potatoes work beautifully beside the chicken. Toss them in oil, salt, and pepper, then spread them on the same sheet pan so they pick up the chicken drippings while they cook. The roasted vegetables will finish at the same time as the bird, giving everything a unified flavor without extra cleanup.

You could start with Royal Canin Labrador Retriever Puppy or Hill's Science Diet Puppy; both are formulated for large-breed growth and have solid ingredient lists. Check the protein and fat percentages so Cooper stays lean, and feed smaller meals three times a day to guard against bloat.

At three months Cooper should get three meals a day, spread out so he never eats a full stomach all at once. The amount on the can is a starting point, but weigh him each week and adjust so he keeps a visible waist; a 30-pound adult goal means roughly a cup of dry food per meal now, give or take a quarter cup depending on his activity.

Look for high-quality brands like Royal Canin, Hill's Science Diet, or Purina Pro Plan that specifically formulate their recipes for large breed puppies. These options provide balanced nutrition to support his rapid growth and help prevent joint issues common in Labradors. Always consult your veterinarian to ensure the diet meets his specific health needs.

Monitor his body condition closely and adjust portions as needed to ensure he stays lean and healthy while growing steadily.
